steps.title: AVAs
steps.body: An American Viticultural Area, or AVA, is a defined grape-growing area with distinct geography. There are over 270. AVAs set boundaries only, not grapes, yields or methods. They can nest: Oakville sits inside Napa Valley, which sits inside the larger North Coast AVA.

steps.title: Labelling
steps.body: A wine naming an AVA needs at least 85% of grapes from it. A varietal name needs 75% of that grape, though Oregon requires 90% for most varieties. A vintage needs 95% from that year when an AVA is named. A state name, like California, needs 100% from that state.

steps.explanation: An AVA only defines where the grapes grow. Producers choose grapes and methods freely.

steps.title: After Prohibition
steps.body: From 1920 to 1933, Prohibition banned the sale of alcohol in the US. Most wineries closed, vineyards were replanted with table grapes or thick-skinned varieties for home winemaking. The industry restarted slowly. Modern fine wine in California really grew from the 1960s, with Robert Mondavi founding his Napa winery in 1966.

steps.prompt: In Oregon, a wine labelled Pinot Noir must contain at least 90% of that grape.
steps.explanation: Yes. Oregon sets a stricter rule than the federal 75% for most varieties.

steps.title: What you learned
points: An AVA defines a place, not grapes or methods
Labels need 85% from an AVA and 75% of a named grape
Prohibition set American wine back by decades
